We recruited participants through social media advertisements and through partner organisations working with high school and university students.

table.text: After the baseline surveys, participants were randomly allocated in a 1:1:1 ratio to Project ABC, Project Personality, or Sharing Feelings by the survey platform, and they were not told which programme served as the control.
Immediately after the programme, participants completed the post-programme survey and received a 100,000 VND voucher (about 4 USD) by email.
All participants gave informed electronic consent before the baseline survey, and the contextual survey of AI chatbot use was conducted with electronic consent under the same programme of work.

Participants were mainly young adults (median age 21; 11% under 18), women made up 59% of the sample with a somewhat smaller share in Project Personality, and participants spent a median of 28 minutes between the two surveys, consistent with the intended length of the programmes, with Project Personality taking the longest (median 31 minutes against 24 and 29 minutes).

Expressive writing about emotional experiences has been shown for decades to produce small improvements in psychological and physical health (Frattaroli, 2006; Pennebaker & Beall, 1986), and our participants told us as much, because being able to share and express their feelings was the one theme that participants in the control raised spontaneously.

We recruited participants through social media advertisements and through partner organisations working with high school and university students.

Eligible participants were aged 13 to 25 and scored 2 or more on the PHQ-2 (Kroenke et al., 2003), the threshold of the original trial, whereas ineligible respondents were directed to a list of Vietnamese mental health resources.

After the baseline surveys, participants were randomly allocated in a 1:1:1 ratio to Project ABC, Project Personality, or Sharing Feelings by the survey platform, and they were not told which programme served as the control.
Immediately after the programme, participants completed the post-programme survey and received a 100,000 VND voucher (about 4 USD) by email.
All participants gave informed electronic consent before the baseline survey, and the contextual survey of AI chatbot use was conducted with electronic consent under the same programme of work.

Participants were mainly young adults (median age 21; 11% under 18), women made up 59% of the sample with a somewhat smaller share in Project Personality, and participants spent a median of 28 minutes between the two surveys, consistent with the intended length of the programmes, with Project Personality taking the longest (median 31 minutes against 24 and 29 minutes).

Expressive writing about emotional experiences has been shown for decades to produce small improvements in psychological and physical health (Frattaroli, 2006; Pennebaker & Beall, 1986), and our participants told us as much, because being able to share and express their feelings was the one theme that participants in the control raised spontaneously.

Moreover, the four-item true-or-false hopelessness measure left little room for change, and we did not conduct the four-week follow-up specified in the protocol, because participants were recruited anonymously online and the attrition typical of online interventions (Eysenbach, 2005) would have left a follow-up sample too small to interpret.
All participants provided informed electronic consent, and the IRB approved a waiver of parental permission for participants under 18

text.text: Single-session interventions (SSIs) are structured, self-guided programmes that deliver one evidence-based component of psychotherapy in a single sitting of 20 to 30 minutes.

In the largest trial of their kind, Schleider and colleagues showed that two web-based SSIs significantly reduced hopelessness and, three months later, depressive symptoms among adolescents in the United States.

However, that sample was aged 13 to 16, predominantly White, and almost entirely female, so whether SSIs work for East Asian young people living under different social, cultural, and economic conditions remains to be determined.

Here, we culturally adapted the SSIs Project ABC (behavioural activation) and Project Personality (growth mindset), together with the placebo control Sharing Feelings, to the Vietnamese context, and tested in a randomised controlled replication trial whether they reduce hopelessness and depressive symptoms immediately after administration.
We show that the adapted programmes were highly acceptable, with ratings matching those of the original English programmes in all three programmes.

Interestingly, hopelessness and depressive 1 symptoms fell significantly within every programme, including the placebo control, and neither SSI produced statistically significant mental health benefits over the control.

Our results therefore underline the challenge of replicating mental health interventions across cultures with different attitudes and stigma towards mental health disorders, as well as different practices competing for alleviating mental distress.
Further studies are required to understand the design principles of digital mental health interventions that are specifically effective for Vietnamese youth.

Vietnam is a young country, with 101 million inhabitants that have a median age of 33 years (Kemp, 2025), and the 2019 census counted 20.4 million people aged 10 to 24, about a fifth of the population (UNFPA Viet Nam, n.d.).

text.text: In our study, we sought to understand whether SSIs are effective in Vietnamese youth, which could give insights into the foundations required for future research into the cultural adaptation of digital mental health interventions specifically tuned to East Asian cultures.
Our randomised controlled replication trial enrolled young people aged 13 to 25 in Vietnam and yielded four main findings.

First, the culturally adapted programmes were as acceptable to Vietnamese young people as the original programmes were to adolescents in the United States, and equally so in all three programmes, which reproduces the acceptability of the original trial.

Second, hopelessness and depressive symptoms fell significantly within each programme immediately after the programme, including the placebo control, so that taking part in any of the three programmes was followed by a small improvement.

Third, neither Project ABC nor Project Personality reduced hopelessness or depressive symptoms relative to Sharing Feelings, with estimates close to zero whose confidence intervals exclude the between-programme effects of the original trial; therefore, the specific advantage of the two SSIs over the supportive control did not reproduce.

Fourth, a contextual survey of the population we recruited from showed that these young people already turn to AI chatbots before friends, family, or professionals when they are distressed, a condition that did not exist when the original trial was run.

Our study therefore underlines the importance of culturally replicating psychological studies and the challenges of doing so, and it paves the way for exciting future research on how digital mental health support should be designed for East Asian youth.
This study was a three-arm, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled trial conducted online in Vietnamese between October 2024 and September 2026 (Figure 1).

text.text: We recruited participants through social media advertisements and through partner organisations working with high school and university students.

Eligible participants were aged 13 to 25 and scored 2 or more on the PHQ-2 (Kroenke et al., 2003), the threshold of the original trial, whereas ineligible respondents were directed to a list of Vietnamese mental health resources.

text.text: Participants under 18 completed a short capacity-to-consent assessment adopted from the original trial, which checks that the young person understands the purpose and procedures of the study, and they could enrol after passing it within two attempts.

After the baseline surveys, participants were randomly allocated in a 1:1:1 ratio to Project ABC, Project Personality, or Sharing Feelings by the survey platform, and they were not told which programme served as the control.
Immediately after the programme, participants completed the post-programme survey and received a 100,000 VND voucher (about 4 USD) by email.
The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Fulbright University Vietnam (protocol number 00125932, approved 12 May 2024).
All participants gave informed electronic consent before the baseline survey, and the contextual survey of AI chatbot use was conducted with electronic consent under the same programme of work.
For minors, the IRB approved a waiver of parental permission following the procedure of the original trial.

The waiver was justified on the grounds that the study recruits adolescents with elevated depressive symptoms, some of whom have strained relationships with their parents or parents who would, for reasons of stigma, prevent them from seeking support, so that requiring parental permission would expose them to distress and would keep away precisely those who stand to benefit most; moreover, parental permission cannot be verified in an online study, and the large gap in mental health knowledge between Vietnamese young people and their parents means that parental permission would not in itself constitute informed consent.

In its place, the protocol substituted developmentally appropriate consent materials, the individual capacity-to-consent assessment described above, access to Vietnamese mental health resources and to the investigators throughout the study, and programmes that have been shown to be safe in adolescents with moderate to high symptoms.

The approach is consistent with the mature-minor provisions under which adolescents in most states of the United States may consent to mental health care on their own (Sharko et al., 2022), which served as the legal reference for the study in the absence of specific informed consent legislation in Vietnam.

text.text: Project ABC (Action Brings Change) teaches behavioural activation, namely that actions shape feelings and that connecting with people, pursuing meaningful goals, and enjoying solitary activities can reverse a negative spiral, whereas Project Personality teaches that personality and emotional responses can change because the brain changes with experience.
Sharing Feelings, the active control of the original trial, is matched in length, format, and number of writing exercises, and it encourages emotional expression without teaching a specific skill.

We followed the framework the developers used for their community and Spanish-language versions of the programmes (Shroff et al., 2023) and the general framework for adapting scalable psychological interventions (Heim & Kohrt, 2019).

text.text: We translated all programme text under the supervision of the principal investigators, and they kept the structure and the number of activities unchanged so that the three programmes remained matched.
Mental health concepts that were ambiguous to Vietnamese youth were resolved with an expert panel of Vietnamese psychologists and translators.

Next, the peer stories and testimonials were rewritten around situations familiar to Vietnamese students, and the audio testimonials were re-recorded by Vietnamese young people with northern, central, and southern accents.
Finally, we piloted the adapted programmes on a small sample of high school and university students (data not shown) and, in consultation with the developer, judged them suitable for the trial.
The programmes were offered to participants under the project name "Kudos".

The schematic follows the design figure of the approved protocol, with the translation and adaptation phase (I) before the trial, the steps of the randomised controlled trial (II to VI), and the analysis phase (VII) after it, and the number of sessions at each stage is taken from the survey-platform export.

The export contains only the 506 sessions that completed both the baseline and the post-programme survey between 7 October 2024 and 19 September 2026, so visitors who were ineligible, declined consent, or stopped before the post-programme survey are not counted.

The ninecheck data integrity screen described in the Methods removed 151 sessions (30%), and one further participant reported an age of 26, outside the protocol range, leaving 354 valid responders (99 in Sharing Feelings, 127 in Project ABC, and 128 in Project Personality).
Vietnamese versions of all instruments were supplied by the study's counselling advisor through the University of Medicine and Pharmacy, Ho Chi Minh City.

Because eligibility was self-reported, the voucher was gifted on completion, and the programme ran unsupervised, we checked data integrity in two stages, both specified after data collection and before any outcome analysis, drawing on the insufficient-effortresponding and internet-fraud literatures (Chandler & Paolacci, 2017; Curran, 2016; Huang et al., 2012; Meade & Craig, 2012; Teitcher et al., 2015).

text.text: Stage 1 screened every recorded session for duplicate, fraudulent, and careless responding and removed the sessions that failed, whereas stage 2 audited the quality of data entry among the sessions that remained and tested whether any residual signal altered the results.
The following nine checks were applied in sequence to the 506 sessions in the platform export, so that a session is counted under the first check it fails: 1.
Duplicate enrolment: a second or later session from the same email address (the first session was kept in the programme to which it was randomised).
Study-team test session: a session entered by a named member of the study team.
Age inconsistency: a four-digit birth year embedded in the email address implying an age more than three years from the stated age.
Duplicate response pattern: baseline answers identical on all 21 items (10 CDI-SF, 7 GAD-7, and 4 BHS-4 items) to those of another session enrolled the same day (the later session was removed).
Impossible programme timing: the post-programme survey opened within five minutes of the baseline submission, which is shorter than any of the three programmes can be completed in.
Speeding on the post-programme survey: completed in under 60 seconds.
Speeding on the baseline survey: completed in under 90 seconds.
Self-reported low effort: the PFS item "I tried my hardest" rated 1 or 2 of 5.9.
Straight-lining of the outcome scale: the same response to all 10 CDI-SF items at baseline or after the programme, which is incoherent given the reversed items.

Checks 5 to 7 require usable timestamps; however, for 42 sessions the platform recorded the post-programme survey as created before the baseline survey ended, so these checks could not be applied, and the sessions were retained and examined in a sensitivity analysis.
We also read all open-ended answers for nonsense or gibberish, as in the original trial, and found none.
Finally, participants outside the protocol's age range of 13 to 25 were excluded.

Of the 506 sessions recorded between 7 October 2024 and 19 September 2026, 151 did not pass the screen and one further participant reported an age of 26, leaving 354 valid responders (Figure 1 and Table 1).

text.text: Stage 2: within-sample data quality audit.

Next, we examined the 354 valid responders with the following checks (Curran, 2016; Meade & Craig, 2012), which served to describe the quality of data entry and to define a residual-signal sensitivity analysis rather than to exclude further participants.
text.formatted: Next, we examined the 354 valid responders with the following checks <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Curran, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Meade & Craig, 2012)</ref>, which served to describe the quality of data entry and to define a residual-signal sensitivity analysis rather than to exclude further participants.

text.text: Range and completeness: every item response was checked against its permitted range and for missing values (none out of range; none missing).

Duplicates within the analysis set: identical 21-item baseline response vectors on any day (6 pairs, 12 participants, of whom 6 were also identical across the full 42-item battery before and after the programme), judged against the distribution of pairwise differences, in which a further 33 pairs differed on one item and 72 on two, so that identical pairs are expected in a sample concentrated near the ceiling of the hopelessness scale.
Normalised names were also compared: 19 names were shared by 45 participants and 8 name-and-age combinations by 16 participants, all with different email addresses and answers.

Straight-lining: the same response to every item of a scale (CDI-SF, none before or after the programme; GAD-7, 18 participants, 5%, 17 of them rating every item 2; PFS, 25 participants, 7%, 23 of them rating every item 5; the whole 21-item baseline battery, none), and the longest run of identical consecutive answers across the baseline battery (median 4 items; 10 participants with a run of 10 or more, and 2 after the programme).

Intra-individual response variability: the standard deviation of each participant's standardised responses across the 17 polytomous baseline items, flagging the lowest 5% (18 participants below 0.63).

Psychometric synonyms: the within-person correlation across the 11 item pairs that correlated at r = 0.40 or more in the sample (median 0.31; negative for 69 participants; undefined for 22 whose answers did not vary).
Multivariate outliers: the Mahalanobis distance of each baseline profile from the sample centroid against the chi-square criterion at p = 0.001 (4 participants).
Internal consistency: Cronbach's alpha for each scale, overall and by programme, with item-rest correlations and the even-odd split-half correlation of the CDI-SF.

Alpha was 0.82 and 0.83 for the CDI-SF before and after the programme, 0.82 for the GAD-7, 0.76 and 0.79 for the BHS-4, and 0.66 for the PFS, with values by programme of 0.75 to 0.86 for the outcome and anxiety scales and 0.60 to 0.71 for the PFS, and the CDI-SF split-half correlation was 0.74.

Identity of answers before and after the programme: identical item responses on both outcome scales (209 participants, 59%; 62%, 57%, and 59% by programme), who spent as long on the post-programme survey as those whose answers changed (median 4.2 against 3.5 minutes, p = 0.20).

Residual-signal sensitivity analysis: the main models were repeated after excluding every participant with a shared name and age, GAD-7 straight-lining, a run of 10 or more identical answers, a negative psychometric synonym index, or an outlying baseline profile (103 excluded, n = 251), and after excluding the later member of each identical baseline pair (n = 348).
The analysis set comprised all valid responders with BHS-4 and CDI-SF scores at both time points.

Within-programme change (after minus before) is summarised with means and 95% confidence intervals and tested with paired t-tests, with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests as a distribution-free check and Holm adjustment within each outcome as a sensitivity check; in addition, the proportions whose score fell, stayed the same, or rose are reported, and change scores were compared between programmes with Welch's t-tests and one-way ANOVA, overall and within each gender.

The pre-specified model for each outcome was a linear regression of the post-programme score on condition (control as reference), baseline score, and age, with heteroscedasticity-robust (HC3) standard errors (Vickers & Altman, 2001).

text.text: Four contrasts were estimated, namely each SSI versus control, both SSIs pooled versus control, and Project ABC versus Project Personality, and the adjusted differences were converted to Cohen's d by dividing by the pooled baseline standard deviation, with the sign reversed so that positive values favour the SSI, as in the original trial.

Mann-Whitney tests on change scores provided a distribution-free check, and default Jeffreys-Zellner-Siow Bayes factors on change scores (Rouder et al., 2009; prior scale 0.707) quantified support for the null (BF01).

text.text: Exploratory moderation by gender, age (under 18 versus 18 and over, and continuous age), baseline hopelessness (two or more statements endorsed), and baseline anxiety (GAD-7 of 10 or more) was tested with interaction terms, and subgroup estimates are reported.

Sensitivity analyses repeated the models in the unscreened sessions (duplicate and test sessions removed), without the age covariate, with gender added as a covariate, without the sessions with unusable timestamps, and with the one participant outside the age range included.
Acceptability was compared between programmes with Welch's t-tests and one-way ANOVA.

The answers to the two open-ended feedback questions were coded into themes with Vietnamese keyword rules that we developed by reading all answers and refined by reviewing the matches and the unmatched answers; an answer could carry several themes, and the percentage of respondents mentioning each theme is reported overall and by programme.

With 99 participants in the control group and 127 to 128 in each SSI group, the trial had 80% power to detect d = 0.38 for a single contrast and d = 0.33 for the pooled contrast, and 49% to 55% power for the original trial's immediate hopelessness effects.

It is reported briefly as context for the population the trial drew on.

text.text: Before testing the programmes, we sought to determine how much of the data collected by an unsupervised, incentivised online trial could be trusted, and the answer was sobering: of the 506 sessions that completed both surveys, 151 (30%) failed at least one of the nine integrity checks, most often because the post-programme survey had been opened within five minutes of the baseline submission, a time in which none of the programmes can be completed.

However, the failures did not differ between programmes (33%, 25%, and 32%; p = 0.24), so the screen did not bias the comparison, and the 354 valid responders who remained were well balanced on age, screening score, and baseline anxiety.

Participants were mainly young adults (median age 21; 11% under 18), women made up 59% of the sample with a somewhat smaller share in Project Personality, and participants spent a median of 28 minutes between the two surveys, consistent with the intended length of the programmes, with Project Personality taking the longest (median 31 minutes against 24 and 29 minutes).

Moreover, the Vietnamese instruments performed well, since Cronbach's alpha was 0.82 and 0.83 for the CDI-SF before and after the programme, 0.76 and 0.79 for the BHS-4, and 0.82 for the GAD-7, adequate in every programme and close to the values reported for the original trial (CDI-SF 0.77 and 0.85, BHS-4 0.84 and 0.87, GAD-7 0.89; Schleider et al., 2022). 28 (22 to 35) Valid responders are the sessions that passed the nine-check data integrity screen described in the Methods and whose stated age lay within the protocol's range of 13 to 25 (participant flow in Figure 1), and percentages are of analysed participants.

text.text: We first asked whether Vietnamese young people would accept programmes that were written for American teenagers and translated into their language and their situations.

Acceptability was high and uniform, since the mean PFS score exceeded 4.5 of 5 in every programme, far above the developers' threshold of 3, and the three programmes did not differ from one another (Figure 2).

text.text: Notably, the placebo control was rated as highly as the two SSIs, so the adapted materials were received as credible programmes rather than as translations.
To understand what lay behind these ratings, we next investigated the answers to the two open-ended feedback questions by coding them into themes (Figure 3).

text.text: When asked what they liked most, participants most often named the hopeful message that feelings and thoughts can change, the relatable stories and situations drawn from Vietnamese school and family life, the gentle and professional tone, and the help in understanding their emotions and their brain.

Interestingly, the themes followed the content of the programmes, because the message of change was named most often in the two SSI programmes, the understanding of how the brain changes most often in Project Personality, and being able to share and express one's feelings almost exclusively in the Sharing Feelings control, where one participant in seven volunteered it ("the programme helped me express my true thoughts"; "I learned that it is not only me, many people are like me").

When asked what they would change, more than half of the participants asked for nothing or simply praised the programme, and a further one in six answered with a personal resolution rather than a change to the programme ("I will try to change my own way of thinking").
The changes that were requested were more examples and stories, more interaction, games, or videos, a shorter programme with less text, and a wider reach to other age groups and to parents.

Moreover, a small number of participants asked for the Vietnamese elements to go deeper still, for example by combining family and traditional values with self-care, and a few would have preferred to take part offline because the online format did not let them say everything they were thinking.

text.text: We next sought to determine whether the programmes changed how participants felt.
Interestingly, both self-reported hopelessness and depressive symptoms declined significantly immediately after the programme in all three programmes, including the placebo control (Figure 4).
text.formatted: Interestingly, both self-reported hopelessness and depressive symptoms declined significantly immediately after the programme in all three programmes, including the placebo control (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">4</ref>).

text.text: The falls were small, about a tenth to a fifth of a pessimistic statement on the BHS-4 and about half a point on the CDI-SF, and they were also remarkably uniform, because the size of the fall did not differ between programmes on either outcome.

The same pattern held when we looked at women and men separately, where the within-programme falls were of similar size in both genders and reached significance in four of the twelve gender-specific comparisons (hopelessness in women in Project Personality and in men in Project ABC; depressive symptoms in women in the control and in women in Project ABC), with no between-programme difference in either gender.

Surprisingly, most participants did not change their answers at all: 43% had endorsed all four pessimistic statements at baseline, 87% gave exactly the same hopelessness total after the programme as before, and two thirds gave the same CDI-SF total, so that the mean change was carried by a minority who moved by one or two points.

Consistent with this, reliable improvement on the CDI-SF (5 points or more) occurred in 2% to 5% of participants per programme and reliable worsening in 0% to 2%, with no difference between programmes.

Because the control group improved as much as the two SSI groups, these within-programme falls cannot be attributed to the content of the programmes; therefore, the baseline-adjusted between-programme contrasts in the next section are the test of the interventions.

The finding stands in contrast to the original trial, in which both SSIs reduced hopelessness relative to Sharing Feelings (Schleider et al., 2022), and it suggests that cultural differences in what the control condition means to participants may account for the discrepancy (see Discussion).

text.text: Participants valued the hopeful message, the relatable stories, and the gentle tone, and more than half asked for nothing to change.
Themes were coded from the two open-ended questions of the post-programme survey for all 354 valid responders (354 answers to "What did you like most about the programme?"
and 350 to "What would you change about the programme?").

Bars show the percentage of all respondents whose answer mentioned each theme, and markers show the percentage within Sharing Feelings (n = 99), Project ABC (n = 127), and Project Personality (n = 128); an answer could carry several themes, so percentages do not sum to 100.

Being able to share and express feelings was named by 14% of participants in Sharing Feelings against 1% in Project ABC and 0% in Project Personality, the hopeful message of change was named by 27%, 44%, and 38%, and the understanding of emotions, thoughts, and the brain by 23%, 26%, and 34%, respectively.

The central question we sought to answer was whether either SSI added anything beyond the supportive control, because this between-programme difference, rather than the change within each programme, is what the original trial reported and what our trial was designed to replicate.

However, after adjusting for the baseline score and age, our data showed that the differences between each SSI and Sharing Feelings were close to zero for hopelessness and, for depressive symptoms, even pointed slightly in the direction of the control (Figure 5).
text.formatted: However, after adjusting for the baseline score and age, our data showed that the differences between each SSI and Sharing Feelings were close to zero for hopelessness and, for depressive symptoms, even pointed slightly in the direction of the control (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">5</ref>).

text.text: Moreover, the confidence intervals of the hopelessness contrasts exclude effects as large as those of the original trial (d = 0.26 and 0.28), the two SSIs did not differ from each other, distribution-free tests agreed, and the Bayes factors favoured no difference over a difference by between three and six to one for hopelessness and by six to seven to one for depressive symptoms.

Collectively, our data therefore indicate not merely an inconclusive result but positive evidence that, in this sample, the two SSIs performed no better than a programme that simply invites young people to share their feelings.

We set out to replicate, in Vietnamese young people, the largest randomised trial of selfguided single-session interventions, and our data reveal three main findings.

First, the cultural adaptation succeeded on its own terms, because Vietnamese young people understood, liked, and endorsed the programmes, with ratings equal to those of the original English programmes.
Second, and intriguingly, hopelessness and depressive symptoms fell significantly within every programme immediately after participation, including the Sharing Feelings control.
Third, neither Project ABC nor Project Personality reduced hopelessness or depressive symptoms relative to the control.
In what follows, we consider why a replication that succeeded in acceptability could have failed in efficacy.
The most striking feature of our data is that the control worked as well as the interventions, and we believe this could be due to the cultural meaning of the control itself.
Sharing Feelings was designed as a placebo for American adolescents, for whom talking about emotions is ordinary.

Vietnamese culture, by contrast, prizes emotional restraint, because expressing negative feelings openly is widely regarded as a loss of face and as a burden on the family (Matsumoto et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Vietnamese culture, by contrast, prizes emotional restraint, because expressing negative feelings openly is widely regarded as a loss of face and as a burden on the family <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Matsumoto et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Yang et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: For a young Vietnamese person, therefore, a structured half hour spent naming and writing about one's own feelings may be anything but inert.

Expressive writing about emotional experiences has been shown for decades to produce small improvements in psychological and physical health (Frattaroli, 2006; Pennebaker & Beall, 1986), and our participants told us as much, because being able to share and express their feelings was the one theme that participants in the control raised spontaneously.

text.text: Consequently, if simply expressing feelings produced a measurable effect on wellbeing in this population, the gap between the SSIs and the control would shrink even when the SSIs were working.

We also cannot rule out that the common factors shared by all three programmes, such as the expectation of benefit (Wampold, 2015), together with regression to the mean and the repetition of the same questionnaires within half an hour (Barnett et al., 2005), contributed to the uniform decline.

text.text: A second possibility concerns what the SSIs ask of their users, because the BEST framework presupposes a minimal degree of mental health awareness and education.

Its brain-science element assumes that a young person already frames low mood as something the brain does and that can be changed, and its saying-is-believing exercises assume a vocabulary in which to explain depressive thinking to a hypothetical peer.

In Vietnam, however, these assumptions cannot be taken for granted, since community members describe depression as stress or as "thinking too much" and rarely use the clinical word (Niemi et al., 2010; van der Ham et al., 2011), and public mental health literacy is low (Dang et al., 2020; Mobashery et al., 2024; Nguyen Thai & Nguyen, 2018).

text.text: We therefore consider it conceivable that the specific ingredients that distinguish the SSIs from Sharing Feelings would have been understood as interesting information rather than converted into new beliefs within 25 minutes.
If this interpretation were right, the BEST elements could need an additional on-ramp in settings like Vietnam that builds the vocabulary before the skill is taught.
A third consideration is a confounder that did not exist when the original trial was run.

Our contextual survey shows that the young people this trial drew on already turn to AI chatbots before friends, family, or professionals when they are distressed, and a similar pattern has recently been reported among adolescents and young adults in the United States (McBain et al., 2026).

text.text: Against a background of daily, unlimited, and responsive conversations with a large language model, the added benefit of a 25-minute structured programme would be difficult to detect.
Fourth, Vietnam is a spiritual country, and we believe that digital interventions compete with other, long-established ways of relieving distress.

Visiting a temple, consulting an astrologer, or seeking out a spirit medium are common responses to emotional difficulty (Jellema, 2007; Nguyen, 2014), and these practices offer something the SSIs in their current form do not, namely a framing of distress and recovery that is rooted in the person's own culture.

text.text: We therefore regard culturally grounded framings of the SSI content, rather than translated ones, as an obvious next step.

Our sample was mainly young adults, whereas the programmes were written for 13 to 16 year olds, and the exploratory signal for Project ABC among the 38 participants under 18 rests on too few participants to be more than a hypothesis for the next trial.

Moreover, the four-item true-or-false hopelessness measure left little room for change, and we did not conduct the four-week follow-up specified in the protocol, because participants were recruited anonymously online and the attrition typical of online interventions (Eysenbach, 2005) would have left a follow-up sample too small to interpret.

text.text: All three programmes were followed by a small improvement in mood among young people who often rarely have anyone to talk to about such issues.

We believe, therefore, that any intervention that gives Vietnamese young people a safe, structured opportunity to express their feelings could be effective, and that the design principles behind the SSIs could be carried into the tools these young people already use.

A chatbot that is deliberately designed around these frameworks, rather than left to improvise, may well prove more effective than either a static programme or an unguided chatbot, and future experiments in our group will investigate precisely this.
